title: Directions and Distance Reasoning — Part 5 of 10

questions.question: What does 'spatial language parsing' involve?
options: Extracting direction, distance, and position information from a natural-language description
Drawing a map by hand
Only extracting numbers, regardless of context
Converting text into a different language
questions.rationale: Spatial language parsing identifies and extracts the direction, distance, and position information embedded in a natural-language problem statement.

questions.question: What is a 'spatial AST' (structured representation)?
options: A physical map
A type of compass
A structured internal model of the parsed spatial entities and their relationships, similar in spirit to the temporal AST in clock reasoning
A distance measured in a specific unit
questions.rationale: A spatial AST is a structured internal representation of the parsed entities and spatial relationships, mirroring the same structured-representation idea used in clock and blood relation reasoning.

questions.question: What is a 'spatial intermediate representation' used for?
options: Displaying the final answer only
Holding the parsed, normalized spatial data in a consistent form before reasoning or constraint-solving is applied
Storing only distances, never directions
Replacing the need for a spatial graph
questions.rationale: The intermediate representation holds the parsed and normalized spatial data consistently, providing a stable structure for the reasoning and constraint-solving stages that follow.

questions.question: What does a 'complete reasoning pipeline' for direction-and-distance problems typically include?
options: Only a single calculation step
Parsing, building a spatial representation, applying constraints, and producing a verified final answer
Only image processing, no text parsing
Only unit conversion
questions.rationale: A complete pipeline chains together parsing, building a structured spatial representation, applying/solving constraints, and verifying the final answer.

questions.question: What role does a 'spatial reasoning engine' play?
options: It coordinates parsing, representation-building, constraint solving, and output formatting into one consistent process
It only draws diagrams
It replaces the need for coordinates
It only works for 3D problems
questions.rationale: The spatial reasoning engine is the overall system tying together every stage of the pipeline into one coherent, repeatable process.

questions.question: Why is 'unit conversion' important in direction-and-distance problems?
options: It never matters
Because directions always need to be converted to degrees
Because distances may be given in different units (km, m, miles) that must be converted to a common unit before combining them
Because unit conversion only applies to time, not distance
questions.rationale: Distances stated in different units must be converted to a shared unit before being added or compared, or the resulting total will be numerically wrong.

questions.question: What does a 'unit-aware representation' help prevent?
options: Nothing useful
Silently combining distances given in different units without converting them first
Direction errors only
The need for a spatial graph
questions.rationale: A unit-aware representation tracks each value's unit explicitly, preventing values in different units from being silently combined without proper conversion.

questions.question: Why is separating parsing from reasoning (rather than doing both at once) a good design principle?
options: It isn't a good principle, they should always be combined
It only applies to time-based problems
It removes the need for verification entirely
It keeps each stage focused on one job, making the overall process easier to verify and debug
questions.rationale: Separating parsing from reasoning keeps each stage focused on a single responsibility, which makes the overall pipeline easier to verify and debug when something goes wrong.

questions.question: What might go wrong if unit conversion is skipped in a multi-step distance problem?
options: Distances in different units could be added directly, producing a numerically wrong total
Nothing, units don't actually matter
The direction would automatically become invalid
The problem would become unsolvable rather than wrong
questions.rationale: Skipping unit conversion risks directly adding, say, a value in meters to a value in kilometers, producing a total that is numerically wrong despite looking plausible.

questions.question: Why is a structured internal representation preferred over reasoning directly from the original sentence each time?
options: It has no real advantage
It avoids repeatedly re-parsing the same information and provides a consistent structure to apply reasoning rules to
It only works for very short sentences
It removes the need for unit conversion
questions.rationale: A structured representation avoids the inefficiency and inconsistency of repeatedly re-interpreting the raw sentence, providing a stable structure that reasoning rules can be applied to directly.
